grammar.title: Articles
grammar.explanation_pt:
Artigos são um dos maiores desafios para brasileiros, porque em português usamos "o/a" muito mais.

**A / an** → algo **não específico** ou mencionado pela **primeira vez**; profissões:
- "They launched **a** new campaign." / "She's **an** influencer."

**The** → algo **específico**, **já mencionado**, **único** ou que todos sabem qual é:
- "They launched a new campaign. **The** campaign was a disaster." (já mencionada)
- "**The** CEO of the company..." (só há um)
- "**The** internet / **the** environment / **the** world"
- superlativos: "**the** best brand"; ordinais: "**the** first ad"
- instrumentos musicais: "play **the** guitar"
- países com plural/União: **the** USA, **the** UK, **the** Netherlands

**Zero article (sem artigo)** → **generalizações** com plurais e incontáveis — aqui o português usa artigo, o inglês **não**:
- "**Customers** trust **reviews**." (os clientes em geral) ❌ "The customers trust the reviews"
- "**Marketing** is changing." / "**Social media** is powerful." / "I love **coffee**."
- nomes de pessoas, cidades, a maioria dos países, idiomas, refeições, esportes: "**Brazil**", "**English**", "have **lunch**", "play **soccer**"
- go to **work / school / bed / church** (função), at **home**

**Teste rápido:** a frase fala de **algo em geral** ou de **algo específico**? Geral → sem artigo. Específico → the.

listening.title: The power of reviews
listening.context_pt: Uma especialista em marketing digital fala num podcast sobre avaliações online.

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.en: Today, the first thing most people do before buying a product is read reviews. Many consumers say they trust online reviews almost as much as personal recommendations. That's a big change. In the past, brands controlled the message through advertising. Now, customers write the story. A single negative review that goes viral can damage a reputation built over decades. But there's good news too: the brands that respond to reviews — especially negative ones — usually earn more trust. A polite, honest reply shows that there are real people behind the logo.

reading.title: From influencers to "de-influencers"
reading.text: For more than a decade, influencer marketing has been one of the fastest-growing areas of advertising. Brands pay creators — from celebrities with millions of followers to "micro-influencers" with just a few thousand — to recommend their products. The logic is simple: people trust people more than they trust ads. But audiences have become more skeptical. Many followers now know that a glowing review may be a paid partnership, and regulators in several countries require influencers to label sponsored posts clearly. In this context, a new trend has appeared: "de-influencing". Creators post videos explaining which popular products are not worth the money and suggesting cheaper alternatives. Ironically, de-influencing has itself become a marketing strategy, as some brands now position themselves as the honest alternative. The lesson for marketers is clear: in a world full of advertising, authenticity is the most valuable — and the most difficult — thing to sell.

grammar.title: Relative clauses
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Relative clauses** adicionam informação sobre um substantivo:

- **who** → pessoas: "The woman **who** designed this app is Brazilian."
- **which** → coisas e animais: "The phone **which** I bought last year is already slow."
- **that** → pessoas ou coisas (informal, muito comum nas defining clauses): "It's a gadget **that** everyone wants."
- **whose** → posse (cujo/cuja): "I have a friend **whose** brother works at Apple."
- **where** → lugares: "This is the shop **where** I bought my laptop."
- **when** → tempo: "I remember the day **when** I got my first phone."

**1. Defining relative clauses** (sem vírgulas) → informação **essencial** para saber de quem/do que falamos:
"The app **that** I use for running is free."
➡ Quando o pronome é **objeto** do verbo seguinte, pode ser **omitido**: "The app (that) **I use**..." / "The man (who) **we met**..."
➡ Quando é **sujeito**, não pode: "The app **that helps** you..." (❌ "The app helps you...")

**2. Non-defining relative clauses** (com vírgulas) → informação **extra**, não essencial. Use **who/which** (nunca **that**) e nunca omita:
"My laptop, **which** I bought in 2020, still works perfectly."
"Melissa Marshall, **who** teaches communication, gave a great talk."

**Which** também pode se referir à frase inteira: "The battery lasts two days, **which** is amazing."

grammar.tip_pt: Em português usamos "que" para tudo. Em inglês, nunca use **what** como pronome relativo: ❌ "The phone what I bought" ✅ "The phone **that/which** I bought".

reading.title: The products that changed everyday life
reading.text: Some products are so ordinary that we forget they were once revolutionary. Take the ballpoint pen, which was patented in 1938 by László Bíró, a Hungarian journalist who was tired of smudged ink. Or the shopping cart, which was invented in the 1930s by a supermarket owner in Oklahoma whose customers stopped shopping when their baskets got too heavy. At first, shoppers refused to use carts — men thought they looked weak and women thought they looked like baby strollers — so the owner hired actors to push them around the store. In Brazil, an example of a product that changed daily life is the flip-flop. Havaianas, which were created in 1962, were inspired by Japanese zori sandals, and for decades they were seen as cheap shoes for poor people. A clever marketing strategy in the 1990s transformed them into a fashion item that celebrities wear all over the world. The lesson? A good product is important, but the story that people tell about it can matter just as much.

grammar.title: Future forms (revisão avançada)
grammar.explanation_pt:
No A2 você conheceu as formas de futuro. No B1+, use-as com precisão — especialmente em apresentações e no trabalho:

**will + verbo:**
- **previsão / opinião** (sem evidência concreta): "I think AI **will** change medicine." / "Scientists probably **won't** find a cure soon."
- **decisão no momento**: "The projector isn't working. — I**'ll** call IT."
- **promessa / oferta**: "I**'ll** send you the slides after the talk."

**be going to + verbo:**
- **plano / intenção** já decidido: "In this talk, I**'m going to** explain three ideas."
- **previsão com evidência** visível agora: "Look at the data — the temperature **is going to** rise."

**Present continuous:** **compromisso marcado** (agenda): "I**'m presenting** at the conference on Friday."

**Present simple:** **horários fixos** e programações: "The talk **starts** at 10 and **finishes** at 11."

**Expressões úteis para graduar certeza:** will **definitely** / will **probably** / **might** / probably **won't** / definitely **won't**.

**Na estrutura de uma apresentação:**
- Abertura (plano): "Today **I'm going to** talk about..."
- Transição: "Now **I'm going to** show you..." / "Let's move on to..."
- Previsão: "In ten years, this technology **will** probably..."
- Encerramento (oferta): "**I'll** be happy to answer your questions."

reading.title: Why explaining matters
reading.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, millions of people suddenly needed to understand complex scientific ideas: how viruses spread, how vaccines work, what an "R number" is. Scientists who could explain these ideas clearly became incredibly influential, while those who used technical language often failed to reach the public — and misinformation filled the gap. Experts in science communication say there are a few simple rules. First, start with why it matters to the audience, not with the method. Second, use analogies: comparing the immune system to a security team or DNA to a recipe book helps people make sense of abstract ideas. Third, avoid jargon, or explain it the first time you use it. Fourth, tell stories: people remember narratives far better than statistics. Finally, be honest about uncertainty. Saying "we don't know yet, but we're going to find out" builds more trust than pretending to have all the answers. In the future, many experts believe these communication skills will be as important for scientists as research itself.

Good evening, everyone. Have you ever wondered why you feel so tired after a night of bad sleep, even if you've spent eight hours in bed? Today I'm going to talk about something that happens in your brain every night while you sleep.

Think of your brain like a busy city. During the day, the city produces a lot of garbage. At night, while you're sleeping, a cleaning team comes out and washes the streets. Scientists have discovered that during deep sleep, a fluid in your brain does exactly that: it removes waste that builds up during the day.

grammar.title: Linguagem funcional de networking
grammar.explanation_pt:
Networking usa estruturas que você já conhece, combinadas em **funções**:

**1. Abrir a conversa (comentário + pergunta):**
- Comentário sobre o contexto + tag question ou pergunta: "Great talk, **wasn't it**?" / "Is it your first time **at this conference**?"
- Pedir para se juntar: "**Mind if I join you?**" / "**Do you mind if** I sit here?"

**2. Apresentar-se e apresentar outros:**
- "I don't think we've met. I'm Ana, **I work for**... / **I'm in charge of**..."
- "**Have you met** Pedro? Pedro, **this is** Laura. **She's the one who** organized the event." (relative clause!)

**3. Manter a conversa — perguntas abertas** (What / How / Why), não sim/não:
- "**What brings you** here?" / "**How did you get into** marketing?" / "**What are you working on** at the moment?"
- **Comentários de interesse:** "Oh, that sounds fascinating!" / "Really? How interesting."
- **Encontrar algo em comum:** "**So do I!**" / "**Me too** — I've been working in tech for five years."

**4. Encerrar com elegância** (nunca sair sem dizer nada):
- "**I'll let you** go and mingle." / "**I should** go and say hi to my colleague."
- "**It's been** great talking to you." (present perfect!)
- "**Let's** connect on LinkedIn." / "**I'll** send you an email next week." (will = promessa)

listening.title: Networking tips from an expert

lines.speaker: Coach
lines.en: Many people hate networking because they think it's about selling themselves. It isn't. Good networking is about being curious. Here are my top tips. First, arrive early — it's much easier to start conversations when the room is half empty. Second, prepare three open questions, like "What are you working on at the moment?" Third, listen more than you talk; people remember how you made them feel, not your job title. Fourth, don't stay with the same person all night — after ten minutes, politely move on. And finally, follow up within 48 hours. Send a short message mentioning something specific you talked about. That's how a five-minute conversation becomes a long-term relationship.

reading.title: The strength of weak ties
reading.text: Who is most likely to help you find your next job: your best friend, or someone you met once at a conference? Surprisingly, research suggests it's often the second. In a classic 1973 study, sociologist Mark Granovetter interviewed people who had recently changed jobs and found that many of them had heard about the opportunity through acquaintances — people they saw only occasionally — rather than close friends. He called this "the strength of weak ties". The explanation is simple: your close friends usually know the same people and hear about the same opportunities as you. Acquaintances, on the other hand, move in different circles, so they bring new information. A large study published in 2022, which analyzed data from millions of LinkedIn users, found further support for the idea, showing that moderately weak connections were the most useful for job mobility. So the next time you're at an event and feel tempted to talk only to your colleagues, remember: the stranger by the coffee machine might be the key to your next opportunity.
